summary: This specification defines selective disclosure for the payload of a JSON Web Signature, mainly for JSON Web Token claims. A holder can reveal only chosen claims to a verifier while the signature can still be checked.

eli5.summary: Showing your ID usually exposes everything on it. With this, you can cover up everything except what is needed, like your age, and it still counts.

questions: how does sd-jwt selective disclosure work
what is a disclosure in sd-jwt
what is key binding in sd-jwt
what is a decoy digest in sd-jwt
subtitle: Sign a token once, then let its owner reveal only the claims each recipient needs.

tldr.problem: A signed token such as a JWT normally carries all its claims in the clear. A holder who received one token cannot show a verifier only some of the claims while the signature still checks out.
tldr.mechanism: The issuer replaces each selectively disclosable claim with a salted hash (a digest) in the signed payload and hands the holder the matching cleartext Disclosures. The holder sends only the chosen Disclosures, optionally with a Key Binding JWT that proves it holds a private key.
tldr.outcome: Verifiers can check the signature and each revealed claim, but cannot see the claims that were held back. The design has limits: issuer and verifier can still link a credential if they collude.

today: RFC 9901 is a Standards Track document with Proposed Standard status, published in November 2025. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Roles
sections.content:
JSON Web Signatures (RFC 7515) protect JSON data against modification, and the JSON Web Token (RFC 7519) is a popular use of them. When a server issues a JWT straight to a relying party, as in OpenID Connect, it can choose at issuance which claims to include. A newer model separates issuance from presentation: an Issuer creates a token with many claims for a Holder, who later shows it to different Verifiers. A token may hold both an address and a birthdate, and the Holder might want to give one Verifier only the address and another only the birthdate.

This specification supports that with an approach called salted hashes. For each claim that can be disclosed selectively, the signed payload carries a digest instead of the cleartext. To present, the Holder sends the signed payload plus the cleartext of the claims it wants to reveal. The Verifier hashes the cleartext and confirms the digest is in the signed payload. A random salt is mixed in so that a Verifier cannot guess the hidden values.

The primary use case is JWT claims, but the mechanism works for any JSON payload of a JWS.
sections.eli5: A teacher writes your grades on a report card and locks each grade in a tiny box. You open only the box the visitor needs to see, and the lock-marks prove the teacher really wrote it.

sections.title: Issuance, Presentation and Key Binding
sections.content:
The flow has three steps. The Issuer issues an SD-JWT that includes all Disclosures to the Holder. The Holder then presents an SD-JWT, or an SD-JWT with Key Binding, containing selected Disclosures to one or more Verifiers.

A Selectively Disclosable JWT (SD-JWT) is an Issuer-signed JWT plus zero or more Disclosures. Disclosures can be left out without breaking the signature, and any modification to one is detected. An SD-JWT may also hold ordinary cleartext claims that are always disclosed.

Key Binding is optional. When the Issuer wants it, the SD-JWT carries a Holder public key, or a reference to one. The Holder then presents an SD-JWT+KB: the SD-JWT plus a Key Binding JWT signed with the Holder's private key over a hash of the SD-JWT, a nonce for freshness and an audience value naming the intended Verifier. Without Key Binding, anyone who gets a copy of the credential could replay it.
sections.eli5: Key Binding is like a guard asking you to sign your name right now, and checking it matches the signature printed on the card, so a stolen card is no good to a thief.

sections.title: The SD-JWT and SD-JWT+KB Formats
sections.content:
The compact form concatenates the parts, separated by a single tilde (~): the Issuer-signed JWT, then each Disclosure followed by a tilde, then the optional Key Binding JWT. For a plain SD-JWT the last element is an empty string, so the final tilde MUST NOT be omitted. That trailing tilde is how the two forms are told apart: a Verifier expecting an SD-JWT MUST check the last component is empty, and one expecting an SD-JWT+KB MUST check it is a valid KB-JWT.

The Issuer-signed JWT MUST be signed with the Issuer's private key and MUST NOT use the none algorithm. Its payload may hold digests, decoy digests, permanently disclosed claims, a Holder key in the cnf claim (RFC 7800) and ordinary claims like iss and iat. The claim names _sd and ... are reserved for conveying digests. The optional top-level _sd_alg claim names the hash algorithm; if absent, sha-256 is used, and implementations MUST support sha-256.

The Key Binding JWT must have the header typ set to kb+jwt and an alg that is not none. Its payload requires iat, aud (a single string), nonce (a string) and sd_hash, a base64url hash over the Issuer-signed JWT and the selected Disclosures.

The Holder MAY send any subset of Disclosures. It MUST NOT send a Disclosure that was not in the issued SD-JWT or send one more than once.
sections.eli5: Everything travels as one long string with squiggly lines (~) between the pieces, like a bead necklace where each bead is separated by a knot.

sections.title: How Disclosures and Digests Work
sections.content:
For an object property, the Issuer builds a JSON array of three elements in this order: a salt (a string), the claim name and the claim value. For an array element it builds an array of two: the salt and the value. The array is UTF-8 encoded and base64url-encoded, and the result is the Disclosure. The recommended way to make a salt is to base64url-encode 128 bits of cryptographically secure random data, with a new salt for each claim.

The digest is the hash (SHA-256 by default) of the US-ASCII bytes of the base64url-encoded Disclosure string itself, not of the decoded bytes, and the digest bytes are then base64url-encoded. No canonicalization is needed, because the digest covers the exact string the Issuer chose.

Digests for object properties go into an _sd array in the object, and the Issuer MUST hide the original order of claims, for example by sorting the digests. For array elements, the element is replaced in the same position by an object {"...": "<digest>"} with no other keys. A Verifier that receives no Disclosure for such an element drops it from the output.

The Issuer MAY add decoy digests, hashes of random numbers with no Disclosure, to obscure how many claims exist. Recursive Disclosures let one hidden claim contain further hidden claims. The Holder then cannot send an inner Disclosure without the outer one that connects it to the signed payload.
sections.eli5: Each secret is put in an envelope with a random sticker, and only a fingerprint of the envelope goes in the signed letter. Showing the envelope later lets anyone check the fingerprint matches.

sections.title: Verification and Processing
sections.content:
A Holder or Verifier receiving an SD-JWT first splits it into the Issuer-signed JWT and Disclosures, then validates the JWT: the signing algorithm must be deemed secure and not none, the signature must verify, the Issuer must be validated along with its signing key, and the _sd_alg hash must be understood and acceptable.

Next it hashes every Disclosure and finds every embedded digest (_sd arrays and ... array objects). A digest with no matching Disclosure is ignored. A matching Disclosure is inserted: the claim into the object, or the value in place of the array element, and the value is processed recursively. The SD-JWT MUST be rejected if a Disclosure has the wrong number of elements, uses _sd or ... as a claim name, or repeats an existing claim name. It also MUST be rejected if any digest appears more than once or any Disclosure is not referenced by a digest. After removing _sd keys and _sd_alg, claims like nbf, exp and aud are checked, and a missing required validity claim causes rejection. The result is the Processed SD-JWT Payload.

The Verifier decides from its own policy whether Key Binding is required, and this MUST NOT depend on whether the Holder sent a KB-JWT. If required and only a bare SD-JWT arrives, the Verifier MUST reject it. Otherwise it checks the KB-JWT signature against the Holder key from the SD-JWT, the typ of kb+jwt, an acceptable iat window, the nonce and aud, and that sd_hash matches the digest it computes. A Holder that receives an SD-JWT+KB from the Issuer MUST reject it.
sections.eli5: The checker looks at the seal, makes sure every envelope shown matches a fingerprint on the signed letter, and refuses anything that does not fit.

sections.title: The JWS JSON Serialization Alternative
sections.content:
Supporting this format is OPTIONAL. Instead of the tilde-joined compact form, an SD-JWT or SD-JWT+KB can be a JWS JSON Serialization object (RFC 7515) in either flattened or general form. Two new unprotected header parameters are defined: disclosures, an array of Disclosure strings, and kb_jwt, present only in an SD-JWT+KB.

Even in this format, the sd_hash is computed over the compact SD-JWT form, which must be built temporarily from the protected header, payload, signature and Disclosures. Unprotected headers other than disclosures are not covered by that digest and so are not protected against tampering. In the general serialization, disclosures and kb_jwt go only in the first unprotected header.
sections.eli5: It is the same sealed-envelope idea, just packed into a tidy labelled box instead of a string with knots.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The goals are selective disclosure (a Verifier learns nothing about undisclosed claim names or values beyond what other sources reveal) and integrity (a malicious Holder cannot alter selectively disclosable claims without detection). The key points follow.

  • Signature: the Issuer-signed JWT must always be signed and the Verifier MUST check it.
  • Check the hashes: a naive Verifier that takes values from Disclosures without checking digests can be fooled by a Holder who edits them.
  • Salt: each salt must be cryptographically random and chosen independently per claim. The recommended minimum for the random portion is 128 bits.
  • Hash function: it MUST be preimage resistant and second-preimage resistant, and SHOULD be collision resistant. Some truncated hashes in the Named Information registry, such as sha-256-32 and sha-256-64, are unfit.
  • Key Binding: without it a leaked credential can be replayed by anyone, and a malicious Verifier can pass it on. The Verifier must not infer its policy from whether a KB-JWT was supplied, or an attacker could strip it.
  • Validity claims: the Issuer MUST NOT make security-critical content such as iss, exp, nbf and cnf selectively disclosable, and Verifiers must still require them.
  • Claim names: names of permanently disclosed claims, including keys of objects that contain concealed claims, are not hidden.
  • Integrity of the set: in a bare SD-JWT the chosen set of Disclosures is not integrity protected, but in an SD-JWT+KB it is.

The document also recommends explicit typing through the typ header (for example example+sd-jwt) to prevent confusion between kinds of JWTs, and says secure key generation, storage and lifecycle management are the implementer's job.
sections.eli5: The rules are: always check the seal, never trust a loose envelope, use really random stickers, and do not put the important seal-proof facts in a hidden envelope.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses unlinkability, meaning adversaries should not be able to correlate presentations of the same user beyond the user's consent. It separates presentation unlinkability, verifier-to-verifier unlinkability and issuer-to-verifier unlinkability. Batch issuance, where the Holder gets many credentials with the same claims and uses a different one each time with fresh Key Binding keys and salts, can give the first two. Time claims such as iat, exp and nbf MUST then be randomized or rounded.

The RFC is explicit that issuer-to-verifier unlinkability against a careless, colluding, compromised or coerced Verifier cannot be achieved with salted-hash approaches like SD-JWT, because the signed credential itself is shown to the Verifier. SD-JWT also does not meet the security properties of anonymous credentials: colluding Verifiers and Issuers can tell when they have seen the same credential even if no fields were disclosed.

Other points: decoy digests are RECOMMENDED when the number or existence of claims could leak information, at the cost of a larger SD-JWT. An Issuer that issues only one type of credential, or whose identity says something about the user, can itself reveal facts, and the RFC suggests a group of issuers could share a common Issuer identifier.
sections.eli5: Even if you only show one sticker, the card still has a unique serial number, so people who compare notes may realise it is the same card. Using many look-alike cards helps with strangers but not with the card maker.
